implementation_notes: A Rust dispatch table is a collection of function pointers: `HashMap<Op, fn(&mut Vm, u8) -> Result<(), Trap>>` (or a slice/array when the key space is dense), filled with `table.insert(Op::Add, add)` and dispatched with `table.get(&op).ok_or(Trap::UnknownOpcode(op))?(&mut vm, arg)`. What replaces the classic structure is the built-in collections plus the `fn` pointer primitive: non-capturing functions coerce to `fn`, so no boxing or trait objects are needed, and the table participates in ownership like any other value. When handlers need captured state, use a table of `Box<dyn Fn(..)>` or of trait objects; when the opcode set is a closed enum, `match` is exhaustive and the compiler already emits a jump table, so the table earns its place only for open, sparse or runtime-registered key spaces.
pitfalls: Only non-capturing functions coerce to `fn`; a closure that captures anything needs `Box<dyn Fn(..)>`, which allocates and moves the table to the heap - the compiler error is clear, the fix is easy to misread.

Function pointers implement PartialEq but comparing them is unreliable (duplicated codegen units can make equal functions compare unequal), so never key or deduplicate registry entries by fn identity.
`HashMap` pays a hash and a bounds check per dispatch and cannot be const-evaluated; a dense `[fn(..); N]` array indexed by opcode stays in static memory and predicts better in hot loops.
A table of `Box<dyn Handler>` adds a vtable indirection per call and one allocation per entry, so trait objects are for dependency-carrying handlers, not for opcode dispatch.

variants.name: Dense array of fn pointers indexed by opcode
variants.idiom_name: static [fn(&mut Cpu, u16); N] indexed by opcode nibble
variants.implementation_notes: When the opcode space is a small dense integer range, the table is a static array rather than a map: each nibble/byte indexes a `fn` pointer directly (`self.table[(op >> 12) as usize](self, op)`), which is branch-free, allocation-free and cache-friendly, and secondary tables can handle the opcodes that share a prefix. What replaces the classic structure is the same fn-pointer primitive, only indexed rather than hashed - it is the Rust form of the interpreter jump table and it keeps everything in static memory, so there is no registry to initialise and nothing to synchronise. Use it for VM/emulator cores; use the map as soon as keys are sparse, textual or added at runtime.
pitfalls: Every slot must be filled, including the unused ones - an error handler has to occupy the holes, because there is no 'missing key' in an array.
The index is derived from untrusted input, so mask and bound it explicitly; a bad shift or an array indexed by a full word panics at runtime.
The signature is fixed for every opcode, so opcodes needing different state must smuggle it through the CPU struct instead of getting their own arguments.

variants.name: Table of boxed trait objects for stateful handlers
variants.implementation_notes: Handlers that carry state or span several methods cannot be `fn` pointers, so the table stores trait objects: `HashMap<String, Box<dyn Handler + Send + Sync>>` with `trait Handler { fn handle(&self, req: &Request) -> Response; }`, looked up and invoked through the vtable. What replaces the classic structure is dynamic dispatch over the collection - the closest Rust analogue of the object-oriented command/strategy registry, and the right shape for plugin registration because each entry may own configuration or dependencies. Use it when state justifies the allocation and the indirection; use plain `fn` pointers or an enum with `match` when it does not.
pitfalls: `Box<dyn Handler>` is not `Send`/`Sync` unless the trait object adds those bounds, so a registry shared across threads fails to compile until the bounds (and any interior mutability) are declared.
One allocation per registered handler plus a vtable call per dispatch - the price of state, not something to pay for stateless opcode tables.
Object safety: methods with generics or returning `Self` make the trait not dyn-compatible, forcing an enum or a different decomposition.
